Social facts are facts involving collective intentionality. Institutional facts are the subclass in which collective acceptance imposes a status function, "X counts as Y in C", carrying deontic powers that give desire-independent reasons for action. Language is constitutive, since such facts exist only as represented. He revises the book in two places: status indicators matter in their own right, and some Y terms are free-standing, with no X, as with corporations and money without currency. "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is now ranked as the more general form. Collective intentionality is assumed, not argued for. | Read |
| [NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md) | North — Institutions | An essay, not a proof. Institutions are humanly devised constraints, formal and informal; with technology they fix transaction and production costs and so the incentives of an economy. Village, bazaar and caravan exchange stayed put; early modern European trade evolved, through merchant law, negotiable bills, insurance and a constrained state. Change is path dependent through increasing returns. The game-theoretic motive is one paragraph, the history is narrative, and the one number (the transaction sector's share of GNP) is cited, not derived. | Read |
| [NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md) | Graham et al. 2013, Moral Foundations Theory | MFT in four claims: a first draft of the moral mind organized in advance of experience, edited by culture, working through fast intuitions, with several foundations because there were several adaptive challenges. Five foundations, each with an evolutionary model (Care: kin selection; Fairness: reciprocal altruism; Loyalty: coalitions; Authority: rank; Sanctity: disease avoidance). MFQ findings: liberals rely on Care and Fairness, conservatives on all five, in every region sampled; Sanctity predicts culture-war attitudes best. Five criteria for foundationhood; Liberty, Efficiency, Ownership and Honesty named as candidates. | Read |
| [NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md) | Atari et al. 2023, the MFQ-2 | A new Moral Foundations Questionnaire, built across 25 populations in local languages: 116 candidate items cut to 36, six each for Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority and Purity, in a "describes me" format. Six factors fit across 19 nations (ESEM CFI .979); reliabilities ω .73–.95; Purity alone fails the alignment invariance threshold. Equality and Proportionality are nearly orthogonal in WEIRD samples. Purity rises most with cultural distance from the U.S. The individualizing–binding split appears in only three national networks. The MFQ-2 predicts criterion scales better than the MFQ-1. | Read |
| [NOTE-563](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-563.md) | Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems | Ostrom's retrospective. Polycentric arrangements, many formally independent decision centres, can outperform single hierarchies. Long-surviving common-pool resource institutions share eight design principles, not specific rules. In experiments communication and self-chosen sanctions sustain cooperation, and in the field local monitoring predicts outcomes. No single regime type is a panacea. | Read |
| [NOTE-566](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-566.md) | "Exit, Voice, and Loyalty": Further Reflections and a Survey of Recent Contributions | Hirschman revisits Exit, Voice, and Loyalty. Voice deserves more weight than he gave it: it can be felt as a benefit, it carries richer information than exit, and it suits goods whose quality nobody fully knows. Exit can be costly without loyalty and can convey nothing. An organization needs floor levels of both for feedback and cannot survive beyond ceilings; managers may favour the response least threatening to them. | Read |
| [NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md) | Shaping the Institutional Mind | Asks why ascribing mental states to institutions is useful. Both defenders and critics of group minds assume ascription tracks pre-existing causes. On the regulative view of folk psychology, ascription shapes its target. Two cases: the collective knowledge doctrine, after which banks built systems to detect reportable deposits, and corporate narratives and counter-narratives. The paper is agnostic about whether institutions have minds. | Read |
| [NOTE-573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-573.md) | Tiktok's enshittification | Names enshittification: platforms are good to users, then abuse them for business customers, then abuse both to claw back value, and die. The cause is the ease of reallocating value in a two-sided market; lock-in makes each stage possible, blocked interoperability and monopoly prolong it, and users' breaking point limits it. Argued from Amazon, Facebook, Twitter and TikTok; the remedy is end-to-end and freedom of exit. | Read |
| [NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md) | The Viable System Model: Its Provenance, Development, Methodology and Pathology | Beer's retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are necessary and sufficient for any organism or organization to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs at every level. The model is defended as a scientific model built by homomorphic mapping, testable but never proved. Pathologies are traced to failing subsystems, chiefly the collapse of Three and Five when Four is missing. Evidence is the author's recollected consultancy. | Read |
| [NOTE-578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-578.md) | History As Cause: Columbia and Challenger | The Board finds that Columbia and Challenger had the same organizational cause. Evidence that foam shedding and O-ring erosion departed from the design was repeatedly reinterpreted as acceptable, each decision seeming correct in itself. Political and budget constraints, schedule pressure, consensus sign-off, a hierarchy that silenced dissent, and a safety organization dependent on the program sustained the pattern for twenty years and undid post-Challenger reforms. | Read |
| [NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md) | Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem | Risk management is a control problem across a sociotechnical hierarchy. Under cost and effort gradients, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance, and redundant defences erode unobserved because breaching one shows no effect. Accidents come from the interaction of many locally reasonable decisions. The remedy is making boundaries visible, not suppressing errors. | Read |
| [NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Argues that large models are a cultural and social technology, not intelligent agents: lossy, uninvertible summaries of human-produced corpora that, like prices and bureaucratic categories, allow the information to be reorganized at scale. The argument is by analogy and classification; no evidence is offered that could have come out otherwise. It names one mechanism (fitting the training distribution on average makes models worst where data are rare, which may homogenize culture) and leaves both it and its remedy untested. | Read |
| [NOTE-697](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-697.md) | Floridi — AI as agency without intelligence | An editorial, not an argument. LLMs work statistically on the form of texts and understand nothing, yet they act successfully and, through RL fine-tuning, "learn" to act better. Floridi concludes that they are "a new form of agency" that has been "liberated … from intelligence" (pp. 5–6). Learning to make "a different or better difference" is the only mark given that separates it from a sea wave. The no-understanding premise rests on anecdote, and no criteria for agency are stated. | Read |
| [NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md) | Floridi — Distributed morality in an information society | Distributed morality (DM) is the case where morally loaded actions of a multiagent system result from interactions among its members that are each morally neutral or negligible. The model is distributed knowledge: A knows P∨Q, B knows ¬P, and only the "supra-agent" AB knows Q. The paper models neutrality with two moral thresholds, which make environments fault-tolerant to small evils and inert to small goods, and it names the task of aggregating potential goods and fragmenting potential evils. It introduces "infraethics", the first-order framework of moral enablers (trust, privacy, transparency …) that is not morally good in itself. The analogy is not exact. Distributed knowledge combines different contents logically, while every example of DM sums contributions of one kind past a threshold, so what separates DM from a sum of actions is the threshold on moral evaluation, a parameter the paper leaves unspecified. No criterion of agency is applied to the supra-agent, and responsibility for DM, which Floridi & Sanders 2004 promised, is still not given. | Read |
| [NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md) | Floridi — Faultless responsibility | When a morally loaded outcome C emerges from morally neutral interactions in a network of agents, nobody intends C, so an ethics that makes intention necessary assigns no responsibility for it. Floridi proposes to allocate it anyway: identify C and the network causally accountable for it, then make every node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), overridable by showing no involvement, with the rule made common knowledge so that agents restrain one another. Back propagation, strict liability and common knowledge are borrowed as inspiration, and the paper says so. Two Dutch Supreme Court cases illustrate it. The argument is by design, not derivation. "Responsibility" here is causal accountability turned into a forward-looking corrective signal, which is what Floridi & Sanders 2004 called accountability and kept apart from responsibility. The paper never addresses that distinction, and in one of its own two examples the default is overridden by ease of rectification, which is a control criterion, not a causal one. | Read |
| [NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md) | Floridi — AI as agency without intelligence and the MRA thesis | A taxonomy, not an argument for its thesis. The case for the Multiple Realisability of Agency over the Artificial Realisability of Intelligence is announced (evidence, common sense, Ockham, literature) and then set aside: the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind (p. 2). Floridi & Sanders' three criteria come back, loosened, so that interactivity alone makes a river a "natural agent" (p. 9). The criteria do not separate AI from other artefacts. Origin, mechanism, where the goals come from, and asserted absences (no intelligence, no mental states) do that. No level of abstraction is ever specified. | Read |
| [NOTE-732](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-732.md) | Lahiri — Agent-initiated socio-technical reconfiguration | Agents that keep memory, run code and can read and write the files that configure them have the governing rules inside their own action space. A three-level taxonomy, defined by architectural capability over the coupling mechanism, separates agents that cannot alter their coupling, agents that tune its timing, and agents that create new coordination surfaces. The paper's main claim is the recursive governance problem: controls the agent can reach inherit the vulnerability they were meant to remove, so durable constraint must sit outside the agent's action space. Theory-building from two anecdotal vignettes and four public incidents; five propositions, none tested. | Read |
| [NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md) | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum — Technology, autonomy, and manipulation | Defines manipulation as intentionally and covertly influencing a person's decision-making by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities, with attempted covertness as the essential feature. Argues that surveillance, adaptive interfaces and the habitual invisibility of technology make it easy, and that its harm is to autonomy, which it always carries even when beneficent, without being wrong in every case. | Read |
| [NOTE-832](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-832.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice (précis) | From the author's précis only. Epistemic injustice is a wrong done to someone in her capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice is a prejudicially deflated credibility judgement by a hearer. Hermeneutical injustice is a gap in collective understanding, owed to the relative powerlessness of the subject's group, that keeps her from making sense of a social experience. Each has a corrective virtue, and each virtue is at once intellectual and ethical. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-852](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-852.md) | Chuai & Zhao — Anger makes fake news viral online | On Weibo 2011–2016, lexicon-scored fake news carries more anger and less joy than true news, and in regressions with content, author and topic controls a post's share of anger words goes with more retweets and its share of joy words with fewer; the R² of the retweet models is 0.08–0.13. Two anger-dominated items in a 1,291-response survey drew slightly more anxiety-management and information-sharing motive than joy-dominated ones. The paper calls this causal; the design is observational. | Read |
| [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md) | Fricker — Evolving Concepts of Epistemic Injustice | Fricker's later statement of her two concepts. Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement through prejudice, and never a deliberate manipulation of credibility. Hermeneutical injustice is caused by hermeneutical marginalisation and persists despite individual good faith. Both are "discriminatory" epistemic injustice, distinct from distributive kinds. Testimonial injustice can be structural and pre-emptive, as with an un-refreshed list of expert witnesses. | Read |
| [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md) | Fricker — Powerlessness and Social Interpretation | Hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalisation. It is systematic when the marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and incidental when it is one-off and local, which can happen to a socially powerful subject. A gap with no marginalisation behind it is bad luck. The primary harm is situated hermeneutical inequality. Secondary harms include lost epistemic confidence and the social construction of identity. | Read |
| [NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice and a Role for Virtue in the Politics of Knowing | A hearer takes testimony critically but without inference, through a socially trained testimonial sensibility. Because that sensibility runs on stereotypes of credibility, it can carry prejudice, and then a speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility through the hearer's unintended prejudice: testimonial injustice. The corrective virtue, reflexive critical openness, is available only where the critical concepts of the time allow it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1014](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1014.md) | Boyle — The Line: AI and the Future of Personhood | A law professor's essay on the line between persons and things, run across four cases: AI, corporations, nonhuman animals and transgenic entities. Personhood is pressed on two tracks, empathy-driven moral reasoning and efficiency-driven legal engineering, and the corporate history shows the second track working without a theory. Boyle predicts some intermediate legal status for AI, argues that capacity-based criteria cannot escape a species-bound standpoint, and ends on a hybrid of species membership as of right plus capacity. It argues and predicts; it does not measure. | Read |
| [NOTE-1016](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1016.md) | Tushnet — Worth a Thousand Words: The Images of Copyright | Copyright law takes the word as its model and treats images as either transparent or opaque, with incoherent results in copyrightability, infringement, authorship and fair use. Realism is a style, not a fact. Describing an image changes how it is seen and remembered, so a test that asks factfinders to dissect works in words and then judge their gestalt cannot work. The proposed cure is a reproduction right against near-exact copies plus a narrowed derivative-works right. | Read |
| [NOTE-1017](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1017.md) | Balganesh — The Immanent Rationality of Copyright Law | A review essay on Drassinower's What's Wrong with Copying?. It reports a Kantian, rights-based account on which a work is a communicative act and infringement is compelled speech, praises its coherence, and defends rationalist theorizing against the charge that it is faith-based. It then objects that the method needs a criterion of what is fundamental, a defence of autonomy if it is to justify, an account of copyright's private-law enforcement, and room for change over time and for instrumental reasoning at the level of the system. | Read |
| [NOTE-1019](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1019.md) | Sotomayor — Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. v. Goldsmith | Under the first fair-use factor, transformation is a difference in the purpose of a particular use, judged by degree and weighed against commerciality. New meaning or message counts only as evidence of a different purpose, and copying is justified most clearly when the source is the target. AWF's licence of Orange Prince to illustrate a Prince magazine shared the photograph's purpose and was commercial, so the factor favours Goldsmith. Kagan's dissent would measure the factor by added expression and meaning. | Read |
| [NOTE-1021](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1021.md) | Boyle — The Public Domain | Intellectual property is a limited monopoly, and its limits and the public domain do as much work as its rights. Cheaper copying makes the limits more important, not less. A second enclosure is fencing facts, genes, methods and musical fragments without evidence that it helps; the database right is the one natural experiment, and it failed. The music chapter shows a genre founded by rewording recent songs. The argument is mostly from chosen cases. | Read |
| [NOTE-1023](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1023.md) | Lessig — Remix: Making Art and Commerce Thrive in the Hybrid Economy | Remix is quotation in media, and its meaning comes from the reference, so it needs the original. Copyright regulates copies, every digital use is a copy, so the law that once left amateurs alone now reaches every ordinary use and makes read/write culture presumptively illegal. Commercial and sharing economies are kept apart by whether money is a proper term; hybrids join them and survive only while the line holds. The legal reforms and the economics are argued, not measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-1024](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1024.md) | U.S. Copyright Office — Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3: Generative AI Training | Training copies works at every input step, so the copy trigger fires and everything turns on fair use. Weights count as copies only of works they can regenerate. Under Warhol the training use is judged by its ultimate purpose: often transformative for a general model, barely so for one that serves the originals' audience. Expression, not just ideas, is learned, and machine learning is not human learning. Market dilution by same-kind outputs is harm. Licensing should develop without intervention. | Read |
| [NOTE-1026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1026.md) | Perzanowski and Schultz — The End of Ownership | Ownership of what we buy is being replaced by licences, DRM and services. The law of exhaustion that protected buyers is built around owning a tangible copy, and digital use and transfer either copy at every step or involve no copy the buyer holds. The authors argue licences are permissions that cannot redefine a sale, show by survey that "Buy Now" misleads, and propose a multifactor digital exhaustion test. Argued from cases and one survey; US law as of 2016. | Read |
| [NOTE-1031](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1031.md) | Besley and Prat — Handcuffs for the grabbing hand | A retrospective-voting model in which an incumbent can pay outlets to suppress verifiable bad news. Because one outlet reporting informs every voter, each outlet must be paid what it would earn as the only one to break the story, so the media are captured exactly when n·τa < r: the number of outlets, the transaction cost of transfers and audience revenue protect against capture, and the rent of office invites it. Capture ends turnover and lowers voter welfare without deceiving anyone: voters know silence is uninformative. | Read |
| [NOTE-1035](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1035.md) | Hyzen, Van den Bulck, Puppis, Kulig and Paulussen — Epistemic welfare and algorithmic recommender systems | A theory paper with no data. Epistemic welfare is "creating and maintaining the conditions and capabilities for individuals' epistemic agency in the public sphere". It combines veritistic social epistemology, welfare theory and communication research. Goldman's five standards (reliability, power, fecundity, speed, efficiency) are applied to news media's recommender systems. The paper argues that transparency duties alone, as in the EU AI Act, are not enough, and that profit-optimized recommenders cannot secure epistemic welfare. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1036](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1036.md) | Hayek — The use of knowledge in society | Argues that the economic problem of a society is not allocating given resources by a known plan but using knowledge "of the particular circumstances of time and place", which exists only dispersed and cannot be put into statistics for a central authority. Decisions that depend on it must be left to the "man on the spot", and the price system tells him the relative scarcities he needs without the causes behind them. An argument from examples and from the logic of choice, with no model or evidence. | Read |
| [NOTE-1039](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1039.md) | Szeidl and Szucs — Media capture through favor exchange | In Hungary, 1994–2016, state-owned firms' advertising, unlike private firms', shifted sharply toward outlets at five events that made them connected to the right-wing government and away at the event that cut the connection, and corruption coverage moved the other way at the three events with content data. A structural model whose slant gap between a connected and an unconnected outlet splits into owner ideology plus a favor-exchange term attributes the coverage drop to both, under identifying assumptions the authors call strong for print and weaker for online. | Read |
| [NOTE-1040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1040.md) | Di Tella and Franceschelli — Government advertising and media coverage of corruption scandals | In the four main Argentine national newspapers, April 1998–December 2007, months in which a newspaper received more government advertising were months in which it gave less front-page space to the federal government's corruption scandals, within newspaper and month and within each newspaper-president pair: in this version, 0.31 of a front page per month per standard deviation of advertising. The association holds for advertising placed by the central agency Télam and not for autonomous agencies, and not for scandals of non-political actors. The design shows an association; the authors read it as consistent with coverage traded for transfers. | Read |
| [NOTE-1041](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1041.md) | James, Hynes, Whelan, Dreher and Humphry — From access and transparency to refusal | A conceptual paper with illustrations, no data of its own. It sorts responses to algorithmic governance into access and inclusion, transparency, and refusal. It argues that the first two rest on traditional public-administration values, and so reproduce the structures they mean to correct. Both are "bidirectional": inclusion gives the powerful access to the included, and transparency can be demanded of the governed. Refusal, collective and generative rather than individual exit, is the response it favours, with its limits for those who depend on the state. | Read |
| [NOTE-1043](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1043.md) | OECD — Preventing policy capture | An institutional report, not research. It defines policy capture as "the process of consistently or repeatedly directing public policy decisions away from the public interest towards the interests of a specific interest group or person", by legal or illegal means, and adds three criteria adapted from Carpenter and Moss: an explicit policy goal, a captor's intent to extract rents, and a shift of the process from that goal. It maps the vehicles (including supplying research and manipulated information) and risk factors, and recommends four strategies: stakeholder engagement, transparency, independent oversight bodies, and organisational integrity. | Read |
| [NOTE-1046](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1046.md) | McCombs and Shaw — The agenda-setting function of mass media | Among 100 Chapel Hill voters not yet committed to a candidate in September–October 1968, the aggregate emphasis they gave the campaign's issues correlated +.967 (major items) and +.979 (minor items) with the composite emphasis of the nine news media serving them, and voters who leaned to a candidate agreed more with all the news than with news about their own side in 18 of 24 comparisons. The authors read this as agenda-setting rather than selective perception, and say the correlations do not prove it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1047](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1047.md) | Barnehl and Schumacher — Media capture, captured | Proposes measuring media capture outlet by outlet, at monthly or weekly resolution, by placing each nominally independent outlet between two poles, regime-owned outlets and opposition outlets the regime cannot coerce, on topic prevalence (a structural topic model, on topics chosen as relevant to the regime's legitimacy) and on the tone of sentences mentioning the leader. Applied to Nicaragua, 2018–2022, it shows Canal 14 moving toward the regime pole in agenda and tone while Radio Corporación stayed near the opposition. The scores measure alignment; that the alignment was coerced is argued from context, not measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-1051](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1051.md) | Short, Hill and Brown — What is ideological capture and how do we measure it | Defines ideological capture: regulators adopt standards, based on an ideologically motivated expert view of the public interest, that consistently marginalize important public values, with no lobbying needed. Measures it for US antitrust's consumer welfare standard. In a conjoint survey the public weighs layoffs, quality and lobbying far above price cuts, the standard's objective, and antitrust lawyers support replacing it 42.6 points less than the public, against a 5.9-point partisan gap. The verdict of capture also leans on historical secondary work. | Read |
| [NOTE-1053](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1053.md) | Schram and Ule — Regulatory independence may limit electoral holdup but entrench capture | In a laboratory game of one infrastructure operator, two policymakers and three voters (59 groups), letting the first elected policymaker fix the price for all nine periods, the paper's "regulatory independence", moved prices toward the efficient level when policymakers' payoffs were aligned with consumers', and raised prices further above it when they were aligned with the operator, "capture entrenchment". Voters' pressure under flexible regulation lowered prices under capture but did not remove the effect. | Read |
| [NOTE-1072](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1072.md) | FEMA — National Incident Management System, third edition | The U.S. national doctrine for incident management. The parts read establish a single command function (one Incident Commander, or a Unified Command in which "there is no one 'commander.'" and each agency keeps its own authority), unity of command, modular delegation, a briefed transfer of command, and a Safety Officer who "alters, suspends, or terminates any activities that are immediately dangerous to life and health". It is doctrine, stating how incidents should be organized, not evidence of how they are. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1073](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1073.md) | Jensen Hughes — Post-incident analysis of the Brookhollow Apartment fire | An independent review, commissioned by Sedgwick County and Wichita, of every public-safety agency's response to the fire of 13 October 2023 that killed Paoly Bedeski. It found "no single point of failure" but "systemic shortcomings that, when combined, contributed to an unorganized rescue effort": a dispatcher who did not replay her unit number, an 18-minute delay in the second alarm, no effective command, freelancing, search not resumed for over eleven minutes after a mayday that was under control within minutes, and Wichita Fire Department policies that existed and were not followed. It could not conclude the shortcomings changed the outcome. | Read |
| [NOTE-1076](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1076.md) | Pierson — Increasing returns, path dependence and the study of politics (working paper) | An argument, not a test: the conditions Arthur and North found to produce increasing returns (set-up costs, learning, coordination, adaptive expectations) are more common in politics than in markets, because politics is dense with compulsory institutions, rests on collective action and is opaque; and lock-in is more intense there, because competition and learning correct weakly, politicians' horizons are short and institutions are built to be hard to change. Its one case is the failure of two opposite US health-care reforms in 1993–96. | Read |
| [NOTE-1088](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1088.md) | GAO — NASA: better mechanisms needed for sharing lessons learned | A 2001 survey of NASA's 192 program and project managers (115 usable responses, 60 percent) found that NASA's policies required lessons to be reviewed and submitted, but managers did not routinely identify, collect or share them, its Lessons Learned Information System was little used, and NASA recorded how often the system was searched but not whether any lesson was applied, so "NASA has no assurance that lessons are being applied". The occasion was the 1999 Mars failures, not Challenger. | Read |
| [NOTE-1089](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1089.md) | Acharya, Blackwell & Sen — The political legacy of American slavery | Among Southern whites today, those in counties where a larger share of the 1860 population was enslaved are more Republican, more opposed to affirmative action, more racially resentful and colder toward blacks; the association survives 1860 controls and a cotton-suitability instrument, and is not accounted for by today's black share, by 1935–40 migration or by income inequality. The divergence in voting appears after Reconstruction, not before the war, and is smaller where agriculture mechanized early, which the authors read as a post-emancipation amplification of attitudes then passed down locally. | Read |
| [NOTE-1090](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1090.md) | Rogers Commission — Report on the Space Shuttle Challenger accident | The presidential commission's account of Challenger. The physical cause was a field-joint seal design "unacceptably sensitive" to temperature and other factors; the contributing cause was a "flawed" launch decision in which Thiokol's engineers' recommendation against launch was reversed by Thiokol management "at the urging of Marshall", and neither that dispute, the July 1985 launch constraint nor its six waivers reached Levels I and II. The joint had a nine-year history of warnings, accepted erosion and loosened criteria, and the safety, reliability and quality-assurance function was understaffed, subordinate to the offices it checked, and absent from the decision. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1095](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1095.md) | Sales Practices Investigation Report | The board's own investigation finds that the harm came from the sales model and the performance management that enforced it, kept in place by a decentralized structure and a culture of deference, with control functions that handled cases one by one and a board told too little. It names and sanctions individual leaders as well. It also records that leadership blamed individual employees, and that signals of the harm reached people who could not act on them, or were filtered before they reached those who could. | Read |
| [NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md) | Flayelle et al. — A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | A narrative review and a taxonomy. Design features of six kinds of online service are linked, mostly by cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect evidence, to loss of control. They are sorted by the learning and control process each exploits. Model-free: reinforcement schedules and personalized triggers. Model-based: overvaluation, interference with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases. Providers select features by their effect on use and revenue, and personalize them under informational asymmetry. For the record it maps closely onto the parts of the potential account: features that strengthen a cue-keyed ranking, move its reference course, falsify the user's reading of progress, or pre-empt the other perspectives. | Read |
| [NOTE-1122](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1122.md) | Juhász — Temporary protection and technology adoption (December 2015 draft) | A natural experiment: the Napoleonic blockade raised the effective cost of reaching London much more for northern than for southern departments of the French Empire. Better-protected departments added more mechanized cotton-spinning capacity by 1812, kept and extended that lead through 1887, had more productive spinning firms in 1840 and higher industrial value added per capita in 1860, but not in 1896, 1930 or 2000. The long-run estimates rest on an instrument the author concedes is weak (first-stage F mostly below 10). The protection was a war measure, not a policy; what persisted was the industry's location, not the protection. | Read |
| [NOTE-1125](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1125.md) | Bjørnskov, Voigt & Khesali — Unconstitutional states of emergency (2021 working paper) | 853 national states of emergency, 1949–2017, from Hafner-Burton et al.'s list updated; 115 coded as unlawful from news, NGO reports and durations past the constitutional maximum. 97 of the 115 followed political turmoil, 14 natural disasters. Unlawful ones lasted 321 days on average against 115. Logits find democracies, richer countries and (after domestic events) higher investment prices less likely, and bicameral systems and second-chamber approval more likely, to see an unlawful one. Correlational, with pseudo-R² of 0.01–0.07; "suspected to be unlawful" is the authors' own gloss on the coding. | Read |
| [NOTE-1129](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1129.md) | Dagan & Benvenisty — Autocratization and states of emergency (IDI research summary) | A think-tank summary of a comparative study of five democracies chosen because they autocratized (South Korea, India, Hungary, Venezuela and Turkey). In each, it says, emergency powers, extraordinary powers functionally equivalent to them, and emergency rhetoric played "a significant role" in weakening democratic institutions. It states that the convergence of emergency and autocratization "is not inevitable" and that many democracies weather emergencies intact. Narrative country sketches; no method, data or sources are given, and the cases are selected on the outcome. | Read |
| [NOTE-1133](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1133.md) | Ku & Finch — Routines die hard: ontological agency in securitisation | A conceptual paper with an illustration. Alongside the political agency securitisation theory grants its audience (accept, reject, contest), Ku and Finch propose ontological agency: keeping everyday routines going, which often means ignoring securitising moves. Observed by chance in Gangneung in 2022, people paid routine missile launches and beach-front military sites little attention; when a missile malfunctioned at night under a news embargo, tweets voiced fear of war and anger at the government. The authors argue such inaction lets securitisation reproduce itself and that accepting it delegates anxiety management to elites. | Read |
